notes.meaning: Peter tells Christians to strip away bad attitudes like hatred, lying, pretending, jealousy, and speaking ill of others. These sins destroy love among believers and stop them from taking in God's truth. Putting away these old habits clears the heart so it can welcome God's word.

Believers are told to long for the pure teaching of God's word just as hungry babies cry for their mother's milk. God's message gives spiritual food without anything harmful mixed in. Feeding regularly on His truth is how Christians grow toward full spiritual maturity.

Peter reminds his readers that they have already tasted the Lord's kindness for themselves. Having personal experience of Christ's goodness makes believers want even more of Him. A real taste of God's love naturally sharpens our desire for His word.

Christians draw near to Jesus, who is described as a living stone. Earthly leaders threw Him away as useless, but God chose Him and values Him above all. Coming to Him by faith connects believers to the one true foundation.

Believers are also living stones, joined together by God into a spiritual temple rather than a building of stone. In this new house, all Christians serve as holy priests who bring spiritual sacrifices like praise, prayer, and good deeds. God gladly accepts these offerings because they come through Jesus Christ.

Peter quotes Isaiah to show that God promised long ago to place Jesus as the precious cornerstone of His people. A cornerstone anchors and aligns the whole structure, keeping it strong and steady. Anyone who puts their trust in Him will never be disappointed or put to shame.

For those who trust in Jesus, He is deeply precious and brings great honor. But to those who reject Him, the ancient scripture comes true: the very stone the builders tossed aside has become the main cornerstone. God's saving plan cannot be stopped by human rejection.

Christ also becomes a rock that trips up unbelievers and causes them to fall because they refuse to obey God's word. When people reject the Savior, their disobedience leads directly to their spiritual ruin. God has determined that all who reject His truth will face this consequence.

differ.view: God appointed the disobedient to their stumbling and justly leaves them in their unbelief.
God eternally appointed that anyone who rejects Christ will stumble and perish, but He did not decree that they must disobey.

notes.meaning: Peter showers believers with titles once given to Israel, calling them a chosen race, a royal priesthood, and God's own special people. Kingship and priesthood meet in Christ, giving all His followers direct access to God. Believers receive this high honor so they can declare the wonderful deeds of the One who called them out of darkness into light.

differ.view: All believers share equally in the priesthood with direct access to God, so no ordained human priest is needed to mediate between God and people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: All Christians share in a common priesthood through baptism, but this does not replace the ministerial priesthood of ordained priests who offer the sacrifice of the Mass.

notes.meaning: Peter echoes the prophet Hosea to show how completely his readers' lives have changed. Before coming to Christ, they were scattered outsiders who had no standing as God's family, but now they belong to Him. They were once without mercy, yet now they live entirely in God's forgiving love.

Christians are reminded that their true home is in heaven, making them temporary residents and travelers in this present world. Because of this, they must say no to sinful bodily cravings that constantly attack their spiritual lives. Guarding the soul requires keeping our desires in check every day.

Believers are called to live honorable and attractive lives before people who do not know God. Even if outsiders falsely accuse them of wrongdoing, seeing consistent good deeds can change their minds. When God visits those observers with His grace, they will end up praising Him too.

Out of respect for the Lord, Christians are to submit to civil rulers, from supreme rulers down to local officials. God has set up earthly authorities to keep order by punishing wrongdoers and encouraging those who do good. Christians honor Christ when they live as lawful, peaceful citizens in their communities.

God desires that believers silence the groundless attacks of critics simply by doing what is right. Many outsiders spoke out against Christians out of pure ignorance and misunderstanding. Living blameless and helpful lives is the most effective way to shut the mouths of foolish accusers.

Christians are truly free people in Christ, set free from the guilt and slavery of sin. Yet this spiritual freedom is never an excuse to break laws or act wickedly. True Christian liberty means freely choosing to serve God with a willing heart.

Peter gives four short commands that balance a Christian's duties to others and to God. Believers must respect every human being, love their fellow Christians deeply, reverence God with holy awe, and honor the ruling king. Putting God first gives believers the right motive for treating everyone else properly.

Household servants are instructed to show proper respect and obedience to their masters. Peter explains that this duty applies not only to masters who are kind and gentle, but even to those who are harsh and unfair. A believer's conduct does not depend on whether the person in charge treats them well.

Bearing the pain of unfair treatment pleases God when a person does so out of devotion to Him. It takes real grace to keep a clear conscience and not lash out when someone mistreats you. God sees this quiet endurance and counts it as pleasing in His sight.

There is no special credit in taking punishment patiently when it was earned by doing wrong. But when someone suffers precisely for doing good and still bears it patiently, God is truly honored. Enduring unfair trials with a calm spirit shows the difference God's grace makes.

Peter reminds Christians that they were called to endure unjust suffering without revenge, because Christ walked this exact path. When Jesus suffered for us, He left an example like a writing-copy for us to imitate. Believers are called to walk in the very footprints He left behind.

Peter quotes Isaiah to emphasize that Jesus was completely innocent and never sinned in any way. He never spoke a dishonest word or tried to deceive anyone, even under pressure. His spotless purity shows that His suffering was entirely undeserved.

When enemies hurled insults at Jesus, He never answered back with harsh words or threats of judgment. Instead, He placed Himself and His situation entirely into the hands of God, the righteous Judge. Entrusting our hurts to God keeps us from seeking our own revenge.

Christ went far beyond setting an example; He carried our sins in His own body on the cross as a sacrifice in our place. He took our guilt so that believers might die to sin and live for what is right. Through the painful wounds He received, our broken souls are spiritually healed and restored to God.

differ.view: Christ's atonement provides physical healing for the body as well as spiritual healing from sin, offering believers the privilege of bodily healing today.
The healing secured on the cross is spiritual restoration from sin, while physical healing of the body is fully realized at the future resurrection.

notes.meaning: Peter reminds his readers that they once wandered aimlessly like lost sheep in great danger. But now, through God's grace, they have turned back to Jesus Christ, the caring Shepherd who guards and watches over their souls. Following Him keeps believers safe under His loving care.
